@graph.description: Can Raman spectra distinguish nine yeast strains, and does the answer depend on the cross-validation scheme?
@graph.nrr:successCriteria: Strain classification above chance under leave-one-plate-out cross-validation, with a clean adversarial control showing the model is not reading plate identity.

nrr:applicabilityConditions.strainDiversity: three standard lab strains and six knockout strains within two species; the authors note the strains may be too genetically similar to produce detectable spectral differences
nrr:applicabilityConditions.assay: spontaneous Raman spectroscopy, 785 nm excitation, desiccated wet cell pellets on stainless steel
nrr:applicabilityConditions.samplePreparation: wet cell pellets spotted onto stainless steel plates stamped with a 96-well layout and desiccated at room temperature and pressure for approximately 3 h
nrr:applicabilityConditions.replicates: three end-to-end biological replicates, produced by repeating sample preparation and imaging in triplicate with separate cell cultures, physical plates and imaging dates
nrr:applicabilityConditions.processing: cosmic ray removal with the Whitaker-Hayes despiking algorithm, default parameters; background subtraction using a single consensus dark spectrum averaged across all three plates, deliberately not one per plate, to avoid injecting additional batch effects; quality control removing spectra whose mean background-subtracted intensity fell below an empirically determined threshold of 1,000 intensity units; Savitzky-Golay smoothing, then autofluorescence baseline subtraction with ModPoly, polynomial order five; cropping to the fingerprint region 300-1,800 cm-1 and area-under-the-curve normalization; outlier removal within each well by elbow detection on each spectrum's deviation from the group median
nrr:applicabilityConditions.models: random forest with 300 trees, and a support vector machine with an RBF kernel and C = 100; class weighting balanced; scikit-learn implementations; hyperparameters chosen empirically
nrr:applicabilityConditions.metric: multiclass Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), bounded in [-1, +1], where +1 is perfect prediction, 0 is random guessing and negative values indicate systemic misclassification; computed per fold and reported as the median across folds
nrr:applicabilityConditions.note: conclusions are specific to this sample-preparation protocol; desiccation is inherently variable and likely contributes to the plate-level batch effect

nrr:invalidators: a more genetically diverse strain panel in which strain identity survives leave-one-plate-out cross-validation
batch correction applied within each training fold, which would make the corrected estimate valid for unseen plates

nrr:cost.note: 75 spectra acquired per strain across three plates, 248 retained after quality control; no monetary or compute cost is reported

nrr:provenanceNotes: The same spectra and the same random forest give median MCC 0.79 under standard cross-validation and 0.32 under leave-one-plate-out cross-validation. The claim's sign depends on the validation scheme alone, which is why the analysis configuration is recorded in every finding's conditions.
The standard cross-validation result is recorded as refuted rather than positive, and the informativeness rule deliberately does not apply its control requirement to a refutation.
Authors' self-declared limitation carried on the corrected finding: The batch-corrected leave-one-plate-out estimates are not valid estimates of generalization to fully unseen plates.

nrr:conditions.batchCorrection: a linear mixed model fitted per wavenumber with plate identity as a random effect, followed by normalizing residuals by their within-batch standard deviations
nrr:conditions.leakage: The batch correction introduces an implicit train-test leakage, as it applies batch correction once to the full dataset rather than to each training fold separately. For leave-one-plate-out cross-validation this effect is severe, as the batch-effect dimension and the cross-validation dimension are identical.
nrr:conditions.intendedReading: The authors intend the batch-corrected results to describe how much information about a variable of interest is contained in the spectra given full knowledge of experimental confounders, much like PCA or clustering applied to an entire dataset, rather than expected performance on new data.

nrr:evidence.label: Results: Batch correction removed plate-level batch effects but did not improve strain prediction; Figure 5
Limitations and caveats: self-declared train-test leakage
nrr:evidence.quote: The batch-corrected leave-one-plate-out estimates are not valid estimates of generalization to fully unseen plates.

nrr:evidence.label: Limitations and caveats: sample size and strain similarity

limitations: The dataset is small: 248 spectra across nine strains and three plates after quality control, yielding noisy cross-validated performance metrics.

The strains may be too genetically similar to produce detectable differences in the Raman spectra, so the negative result for strain classification may not generalize to collections of strains with greater diversity.

The desiccation step, while necessary to yield a sufficiently strong signal, is inherently variable and likely contributes to the plate-level batch effect; other sample preparation techniques may produce weaker batch effects.

@graph.nrr:note: Both controls now behave. What is missing is a detection limit: the authors state the dataset is small and the strains may be too similar to produce detectable differences, but give no bound on the strain difference the design could have resolved.
